- **Allocating every frame**: new containers, strings and objects built and thrown away each frame.
- **Checking everything against everything**: with n objects, testing every pair is n(n − 1)/2 checks, which grows with n².

steps.prompt: A bullet-hell level has **1000** bullets and enemies, and every pair is tested for collision each frame. How many pair tests is that per frame?
steps.explanation: 1000 × 999 ÷ 2 = **499,500** tests per frame, about 30 million a second at 60 fps. Double the objects and the work roughly quadruples. Most of those pairs are on opposite sides of the screen and could never touch.

steps.title: n versus n²
steps.body: Drag the slider to see how checking every pair (n²) pulls away from touching each object once (n) as the number of objects grows. A spatial grid aims to bring collision checks back toward the n curve.

steps.title: A spatial grid
steps.body:
Split the world into square **cells**, about as big as the largest object. Each frame, put every object into the cell its position falls in: for a bounded level, a `std::vector` of cells indexed by `cy * width + cx` works, and an `std::unordered_map` keyed on the cell suits an endless world. Keep the cells between frames and `clear()` them, so their capacity is reused. To find what might touch an object, look only in its own cell and the 8 around it.

The cell of a position is the **floor** of `x / size` on each axis:

```cpp
int cellOf(float x, float size) {
    return static_cast<int>(std::floor(x / size));   // floor, not a plain cast
}
```

A plain `static_cast<int>` chops toward zero, so −0.25 becomes 0 instead of −1. Physics engines run a *broad phase* like this for their own bodies (Box2D uses a tree of boxes rather than a grid); you need one for your own queries, such as *which bats are near the lantern*.

steps.prompt: Cells are 4 units wide, so x from −4 up to 0 is cell −1 and x from 0 up to 4 is cell 0. This should print `(2, 0)`, `(-1, 0)` and `(0, 0)`. Click the line with the bug.
fixes: Change line 8 to apply `std::floor(...)` to each division before the cast
Change line 8 to apply `std::round(...)` to each division before the cast
Change line 8 to apply `std::ceil(...)` to each division before the cast
Change line 8 to apply `std::abs(...)` to each division before the cast, so negative positions work
steps.hint: What is −1 ÷ 4, and what does a cast to `int` do with −0.25?
steps.explanation: Casting to `int` **truncates toward zero**, so −0.25 becomes 0 and cell 0 secretly covers x from −4 to 4, twice as wide as every other cell. `std::floor` always rounds down, giving −1. `std::round` and `std::ceil` shift every cell boundary (9.5 lands in cell 2 with round but 3 with ceil, and y = 2 moves to cell 1), and `std::abs` folds the left half of the world onto the right half.

steps.prompt: The same 1000 objects are spread evenly over a grid, about **10 per cell**. Each object is tested only against the others in its own cell and the 8 around it, about **90** objects. Counting each pair once, roughly how many tests is that per frame?
steps.hint: 1000 objects × 90 neighbours, then halve it because each pair would otherwise be counted twice.
steps.explanation: 1000 × 90 ÷ 2 ≈ **45,000** tests, about a tenth of the 499,500 before, and it now grows in proportion to the number of objects rather than its square. Ten times more objects in a ten times bigger level means ten times the work, not a hundred.

steps.prompt: Which lines, run every frame, allocate heap memory? (Measured by replacing the global `operator new` with one that counts its calls, at `-O0` and `-O2`, with Apple clang and libc++.)

items.text: `std::vector<Enemy*> nearby; nearby.push_back(e);`
`std::string label = "Sparks collected this run: " + std::to_string(n);`
`auto p = std::make_unique<Particle>();`
`std::vector<int> ids = level.enemyIds;`
`Vec2 offset{1, 2};`
`kept.clear(); kept.push_back(id);` on a vector created once at startup
`std::sort(ids.begin(), ids.end());`
`for (const Enemy& e : enemies) total += e.hp;`

steps.hint: A new container, a long string, `make_unique` or a **copy** of a vector all need a fresh block. Plain values, reused containers and in-place algorithms do not.
steps.explanation: A vector created inside the frame allocates on its first `push_back`; a long concatenated `std::string`, `make_unique` and copying a vector (easy to do by accident with `=` or a by-value parameter) all allocate every time. A `Vec2` is a plain local value, a cleared vector keeps its capacity, `std::sort` works in place, and a loop over `const&` copies nothing. Create containers once, reuse them, and pass big things by reference.

steps.prompt: Ember Run runs smoothly but **hitches every few seconds**. What should Rin do first?
choices: Record the hitch with a profiler on an optimised build and see what runs in the slow frames
Rewrite the collision code with a spatial grid, since collisions are usually the problem
Lower the target frame rate to 30 fps, so every frame gets twice the budget
Replace every `std::vector` with a raw array, since vectors allocate
steps.hint: Regular, occasional hitches have a cause you can see in the slow frames themselves.
steps.explanation: A smooth game with periodic spikes points at something that happens occasionally: a burst of allocations when a vector outgrows its capacity, a file loaded on the game thread, a big spawn wave. Only the profiler shows which one it is. Rewriting collisions is a guess, halving the frame rate hides the problem and makes every frame worse, and raw arrays throw away safety without touching the cause.
